title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Zhiming Wang, Yongqi Liu, Zhaohui Wang, Shanglin Yang, Zikun Li
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.

infographic.key_insight: ServerBench tests whether coding agents can build specialized LLM serving systems that maximize latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Effective serving designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection while preserving session dependencies, latency targets, and correctness.
method: Let agents implement and experimentally optimize complete serving systems against a shared dollars-per-dollar objective.
Use stateful workload replay to preserve session dependencies.
Independently verify submitted systems and compare them with serving baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, 22 of 33 runs produced verified systems and 13 beat the strongest baseline; Claude Sonnet 5.5 reached 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87× the vLLM reference.
infographic.watch_item: Optimization can introduce execution paths that require explicit verification, and 11 of 33 runs did not yield verified systems.
infographic.paper_title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?

title: Energy-Guided Transport for Projection-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching
authors: Giuliano Galadini, Aurelio Uncini, Danilo Comminiello
abstract: Deep generative models, particularly Flow Matching frameworks, have emerged as powerful tools for synthesizing complex physical systems. However, standard architectures remain purely statistically driven and agnostic to the underlying governing equations, often violating fundamental physical constraints during inference. Existing zero-shot approaches designed to enforce these constraints typically rely on rigid algebraic projections. While effective for sparse boundary conditions, applying such discrete geometric corrections to dense, full-domain PDEs may disrupt the probability path, \rev{potentially deviating from the learned manifold and introducing substantial computational overhead}. To address these challenges, we introduce Energy-Guided Transport, a novel training-free framework that formulates non-linear physical constraints as a smooth potential energy landscape. Rather than interrupting the ODE integration, our method applies a continuous dissipative force directly to the intermediate generative states, steering them toward the physical manifold. By evaluating this force implicitly via reverse-mode automatic differentiation, our framework preserves the natural dynamics of the flow while maintaining an efficient $\mathcal{O}(N)$ algorithmic complexity. We extensively evaluate our framework across various 1D and 2D physical systems, including the chaotic Navier-Stokes equations. Our method achieves stable generation without structural divergence, significantly improves the stability-accuracy trade-off compared to state-of-the-art methods, and substantially accelerates inference with respect to exact projection strategies. Code available at: https://github.com/ispamm/Projection-free-energy-guided-flow-matching.

infographic.key_insight: Energy-Guided Transport steers flow-matching samples toward physical constraints using continuous energy-based forces instead of discrete projections.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The training-free approach can improve physical consistency and inference efficiency when generating PDE-governed systems without retraining the generative model.
method: Express nonlinear physical constraints as a smooth potential energy.
Apply a continuous dissipative force to intermediate states during ODE integration.
Compute the force implicitly with reverse-mode automatic differentiation, with claimed O(N) algorithmic complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1D and 2D physical systems, including chaotic Navier–Stokes equations, the abstract reports stable generation, improved stability–accuracy trade-offs, and faster inference than exact projection strategies.
infographic.watch_item: Continuous energy guidance does not by itself guarantee exact constraint satisfaction; residual violations and sensitivity to guidance strength should be checked.
infographic.paper_title: Energy-Guided Transport for Projection-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching

title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
authors: Zhiyong Zhou, Sheng Liao, Youshen Xiao, Xiaolin Li, Yakang Dai
abstract: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.

infographic.key_insight: PINR-ESI reconstructs extended cortical activity from EEG using a physics-informed implicit neural representation without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Embedding the EEG forward model into reconstruction reduces reliance on synthetic training pairs while representing cortical current density as a continuous spatial field.
method: Model cortical current density with a coordinate-conditioned neural field.
Use a classical inverse estimate for warm initialization and spatial constraints.
Project patch-integrated source coefficients through the lead field and enforce agreement with measured EEG.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations varying noise, source count, and extent showed the clearest gains in active-region identification, especially for multiple and larger sources; patient EEG and intracranial stimulation evaluations further supported feasibility.
infographic.watch_item: Dependence on the lead field and classical inverse initialization warrants testing sensitivity to forward-model errors and initialization bias.
infographic.paper_title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging

title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
authors: Mattia Greiche, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maximilian Puelma Touzel
abstract: Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.

infographic.key_insight: Richer context does not produce uniform behavioral effects in LLM social agents; effects depend on the type of enrichment and the model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Validate social-simulation agents for both stability under meaning-preserving prompt changes and appropriate responses to decision-relevant changes.
method: Apply controlled prompt substitutions for neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding.
Define selective robustness as invariance to meaning-preserving variations paired with directional sensitivity to relevant social changes.
Compare agent behavior in a Prisoner’s Dilemma-like game.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation across two models found distinct, model-dependent behavioral patterns across the context-enrichment types.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence from two models and one game setting does not establish that context enrichment reliably improves robustness across social simulations.
infographic.paper_title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents

title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
authors: Fei Lin, Tengchao Zhang, Ziyang Gong, Xiaotong Yu, Bohan Zhang, Yifan Zhou
abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

infographic.key_insight: BEAKER reveals a gap between MLLMs’ coarse understanding of laboratory procedures and the precise, action-grounded perception needed to execute them.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Autonomous chemistry systems need targeted validation of operable regions, feasible trajectories, apparatus states, and safety constraints before relying on MLLMs for execution.
method: Benchmark embodied laboratory capabilities across 11 image and video task types.
Use questions and annotations manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied AI experts, without AI assistance.
Evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples, offline single-turn evaluation finds stronger coarse video-procedure understanding but persistent difficulties with action grounding, fine-grained recognition, and mid-length step ordering.
infographic.watch_item: Offline, single-turn benchmark performance does not establish safe or reliable closed-loop execution in physical laboratories.
infographic.paper_title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories

title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Guoqin Xiong, Shengtao Wen, Xiang Chen, Xinyi Zeng, Zhaoxin Fan, Wei Ye
abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents translate model outputs into consequential actions, turning indirect prompt injection into an execution-security problem. Existing defenses constrain tool calls, trajectories, or information flows, but often leave action semantics, state dependencies, and evidence relations implicit, limiting generalization across heterogeneous tools and complicating safe updates. We present \ours{}, a dynamic ontology-guided governance framework. \ours{} grounds heterogeneous calls in a shared semantic representation and combines an executable ontology with episode-level task state to derive deterministic ready, waiting, and forbidden decisions. A waiting decision identifies an unmet but recoverable obligation, enabling bounded replanning without expanding the agent's authorization boundary. \ours{} evolves its ontology offline from verified training executions. An offline LLM proposes instance-independent action--state axioms, which are accepted only if they address ontology errors exposed by training failures, preserve logical consistency and protected entailments, and pass held-out validation before the ontology is frozen. We evaluate \ours{} on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under benign and indirect prompt-injection settings. \ours{} achieves a 0\% attack success rate (ASR) across all three benchmarks while improving task utility under attack compared with existing baselines. These results show that explicit semantic governance can strengthen execution security without indiscriminate blocking.

infographic.key_insight: SecureGARD governs tool-using LLM agents with explicit action semantics and task state, blocking unsafe execution while allowing bounded replanning for unmet obligations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared semantic layer can enforce authorization across heterogeneous tools without indiscriminately blocking legitimate tasks.
method: Map tool calls into a shared semantic representation governed by an executable ontology.
Combine ontology rules with episode-level task state to classify actions as ready, waiting, or forbidden.
Refine ontology axioms offline using verified training executions, consistency checks, protected entailments, and held-out validation, then freeze the ontology.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 0% attack success rate on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn, with improved task utility under attack compared with existing baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment depends on accurate tool semantics and state tracking; the reported benchmark results do not establish robustness to unseen tools or attacks.
infographic.paper_title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

title: Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man
authors: Xinglu Wang, Edward Wang, Yong Zhang, Zhenan Fan
abstract: Training an agent to play Pac-Man with only up, down, left and right actions raises a basic question: when performance is poor, what should be improved? Difficulty can arise from reading the screen or from choosing actions over a long sequence. We examine these problems in a Qwen3.5-9B-based agent through separate perception checks and primitive-policy reinforcement-learning studies. In the policy study, which uses textual boards to remove image transcription from the decision interface, completion on eight held-out mazes increased from 0% before this optimization to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint, with three extra lives. The perception checks show that accurate static screenshot reading can coexist with errors during interaction. A separate policy comparison also shows that further optimization can accompany worse action choices. Together, these findings motivate concrete checks for post-training: evaluate perception in use, distinguish training success from full-game validation, and examine decisions and later performance rather than relying on one selected score. The study provides empirical lessons for improving future agent training and evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Pac-Man agent failures require separate checks of perception and decision-making: accurate static screenshot reading does not guarantee reliable interaction, and further policy optimization can worsen action choices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate perception during use, validate full-game performance separately from training success, and inspect decisions across checkpoints before deploying an agent.
method: Studied a Qwen3.5-9B-based agent using only up, down, left, and right actions.
Ran separate perception checks and primitive-policy reinforcement-learning studies.
Used textual boards in the policy study to remove image transcription from the decision interface.
infographic.evidence_signal: On eight held-out mazes with three extra lives, completion rose from 0% before policy optimization to 80.2% at a selected checkpoint.
infographic.watch_item: The selected-checkpoint result on textual boards should not be treated as evidence of equally reliable end-to-end visual gameplay.
infographic.paper_title: Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man

title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI
authors: NVIDIA, :, Anis Ahmad, Jon Allen, Malik Aqeel Anwar, Jesse Archer
abstract: We present a shared framework that adapts Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive world simulation in Physical AI. By streaming visual observations in response to actions and scene controls, the framework enables users and embodied agents to interact with evolving virtual environments. It supports both predicting the visual consequences of actions and generating observations from physical state maintained by an external simulator. We demonstrate this approach across camera navigation and robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle (AV) simulation. These examples provide a shared foundation for developing interactive virtual environments for Physical AI training and evaluation. Our code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/nvidia/cosmos and https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/cosmos3-examples. The project website is available at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/cosmos-lab/cosmos-simulation.

infographic.key_insight: A shared framework adapts Cosmos world foundation models to stream visual observations in response to actions and scene controls for interactive Physical AI simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports virtual environments for embodied-agent training and evaluation through action-conditioned prediction or visualization of externally simulated physical states.
method: Adapt Cosmos world foundation models for real-time interactive simulation.
Stream visual observations conditioned on actions and scene controls.
Support action-driven visual prediction and observation generation from external simulator states.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations in camera navigation, robot manipulation, controllable video transfer, and multi-view autonomous vehicle simulation, but provides no quantitative evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: Real-time latency and physical fidelity should be validated before relying on generated observations for training or evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Interactive World Simulation with Cosmos for Physical AI

title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents
authors: Jalaj Bhandari, Dhawal Gupta, Hongli Zhan, Zhenting Wang, Varad Pimpalkhute, Zhengzhong Liu
abstract: In this work, we evaluate a simple inference-time scaling approach based on \textit{turn-level best-of-N sampling} (\method) for large language model (LLM) agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. We instantiate this using a \textit{generator-selector} framework with two LLMs; at each turn, a \emph{generator} model generates $N$ candidate actions and a \emph{selector} model selects one of them, which is then executed in the environment. This paper is closely related to the work of \cite{zainullina2025guided} who used critic models for guided search at inference time. Different from their work, we evaluate if off-the-shelf, open-weight LLMs can be effective at comparing different candidate actions directly. Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks show that \method can lead to significant performance improvements, both in terms of accuracy (5--10\%) and consistency across repeated attempts. Analysis of agent trajectories reveal a shift in agent behaviour towards desirable patterns such as reduction in number of attempts to solve the task, improved task instruction following, debugging and testing.

infographic.key_insight: Turn-level best-of-N sampling improves LLM agent accuracy and consistency by selecting among multiple candidate actions before each execution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A generator-selector setup offers a practical inference-time scaling approach for agents tackling complex, long-horizon terminal tasks.
method: Generate N candidate actions at each turn.
Use a second, off-the-shelf open-weight LLM to compare candidates and select one.
Execute the selected action and repeat.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks report 5–10% accuracy improvements and greater consistency across repeated attempts, with trajectory analysis indicating better instruction following, debugging, and testing.
infographic.watch_item: Generating and comparing multiple actions per turn adds inference cost; the abstract does not quantify latency or cost-effectiveness.
infographic.paper_title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents

title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI
authors: Remi Denton, Aida Davani, Cynthia L Bennett, Michael Madaio, Roma Patel, Himabindu Lakkaraju
abstract: Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift toward long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI reshapes human experience over time. To this end, we map the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being to reveal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture. Ultimately, we advocate for moving beyond simple preference optimization toward alignment strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being by navigating these complex temporal scales.

infographic.key_insight: Optimizing generative AI for immediate conversational satisfaction can overlook cumulative harms to cognition, social connection, and human agency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Alignment pipelines should account for long-term human well-being rather than treating short-horizon user preferences as a sufficient success metric.
method: Map tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs across four facets of human well-being.
Identify longitudinal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture.
Propose a shift from simple preference optimization toward long-horizon alignment.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a conceptual framework and research agenda, without reporting datasets, experiments, or quantitative evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Translating long-term well-being into measurable alignment objectives remains an implementation challenge not resolved in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI

title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
authors: Benjamin Jacob Bodner
abstract: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; https://github.com/BjBodner/amm-optimizer).

infographic.key_insight: AMM uses online landscape probes to route a fixed evaluation budget among classical optimizers, achieving the highest target share in 382 of 600 held-out BBOB evaluation cells, including ties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For continuous black-box optimization, AMM offers an open-source Python router that adapts optimizer choice to landscape structure and remaining budget.
method: Probe curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure online.
Route evaluations among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy engines.
Charge probe costs to the budget and apply dimension-by-budget validity ranges and defaults.
infographic.evidence_signal: A one-time held-out BBOB test covered instances 101–110, dimensions 2–40 and budgets of 10D–1000D against up to seven competitors; AMM led outright in 236 cells and tied for the lead in 146.
infographic.watch_item: Gains were benchmark-dependent: rotating separable functions f3–f4 removed most of the lead, while held-out MA-BBOB showed parity with IPOP-CMA-ES at the final budget and lower anytime performance.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes

title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials
authors: Eliane Younes, Elie Hachem, Marc Bernacki
abstract: Grain growth during heat treatment strongly affects the microstructure of polycrystalline materials and, consequently, their mechanical properties. Although numerical methods such as front-tracking or front-capturing simulations can accurately describe grain growth, their high computational cost limits their use for long or non-isothermal thermal cycles. In previous work, grain growth was successfully predicted under isothermal conditions by treating grain size distributions as time series and forecasting their evolution using recurrent neural networks, allowing complete grain growth trajectories to be generated in seconds rather than through costly PDE-based simulations. In the present work, this forecasting framework is reformulated to handle non-isothermal conditions by explicitly incorporating thermal information into the model architecture. Grain size distributions are encoded using a convolutional neural network, thermal descriptors are embedded through a dedicated multilayer perceptron, and temporal evolution is predicted using a recurrent network. Instantaneous temperature and thermal rate are provided at each time step, allowing the model to adapt its predictions to changing thermal conditions. The framework is trained and evaluated on datasets generated from validated front-tracking simulations across a wide range of non-isothermal thermal paths. The results show that the thermally conditioned model accurately reproduces grain growth dynamics under complex thermal histories, achieving, in k-fold cross-validation over all simulations, mean relative errors of 2.99% (one-hour cycles) and 4.51% (four-hour cycles) with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.99, and mean relative errors between 1.91% and 14.66% on ten simulations following four unseen thermal histories of increasing complexity.

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning recurrent forecasts on temperature and thermal rate enables accurate prediction of grain growth during non-isothermal heat treatment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a computationally efficient alternative to repeated grain-growth simulations for exploring heat-treatment schedules.
method: Encode grain size distributions with a convolutional neural network.
Embed instantaneous temperature and thermal rate with a dedicated multilayer perceptron.
Forecast microstructural evolution with a thermally conditioned recurrent network.
infographic.evidence_signal: On front-tracking simulation data, k-fold cross-validation yielded mean relative errors of 2.99% for one-hour cycles and 4.51% for four-hour cycles, with R² above 0.99; errors ranged from 1.91% to 14.66% across ten simulations with four unseen thermal histories.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is simulation-based, and the higher errors on some unseen thermal histories warrant caution when extrapolating to new heat-treatment conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Thermally Conditioned Time-Series Forecasting of Grain Growth in Polycrystalline Materials

title: From Reconstruction to Imputation: Test-Time Optimization for Missing Time-Series Channels
authors: Björn Ludwig, Alexander Windmann, René Heesch, Oliver Niggemann
abstract: Complete sensor-channel failures create a difficult form of time-series missingness: local interpolation is unavailable, and deploying a separately trained imputer for every failure pattern may be impractical. We ask whether a sequence reconstructor trained without artificial mask augmentation and then frozen can be converted into an imputer at inference time. Our method treats the missing entries of each test window as optimization variables, clamps all observations, and backpropagates through the frozen model to minimize reconstruction error only on observed coordinates. The resulting observed-self-consistency objective requires neither artificial mask augmentation nor full-channel dropout during reconstructor training. We characterize when this refinement is informative through the cross-Jacobian from missing inputs to observed residuals, and use an optional temporal-smoothness prior when that coupling is weak. Across five real-world datasets with exactly one channel synthetically masked per test window and four reconstruction architectures, no-prior test-time refinement reduces MAE relative to one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 dataset-backbone combinations. Compared with mask-aware imputers trained under either standard structured masks or matched full-channel dropout, the best refined reconstructor achieves the lowest MAE on two datasets and trails the strongest baseline on three. These gains require substantially more inference time and are sensitive to cross-channel coupling. Our results establish test-time self-consistency as a conditional inference-time adapter for frozen reconstruction models that complements mask-aware imputation without retraining the reconstructor.

infographic.key_insight: A frozen time-series reconstructor can impute a missing sensor channel by optimizing missing inputs at test time to improve reconstruction consistency on observed channels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a way to adapt existing reconstruction models to sensor-channel failures without retraining, at the cost of substantially slower inference.
method: Train a sequence reconstructor without artificial mask augmentation, then freeze its weights.
Optimize missing entries through the frozen model while clamping observations and minimizing observed-coordinate reconstruction error.
Assess missing-to-observed coupling via the cross-Jacobian; optionally add a temporal-smoothness prior when coupling is weak.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five real-world datasets and four architectures with one synthetically missing channel per test window, no-prior refinement reduced MAE versus one-pass reconstruction in 19 of 20 combinations; the best refined reconstructor beat mask-aware baselines on two datasets but trailed on three.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on cross-channel coupling, and evaluation with exactly one missing channel does not establish performance under simultaneous channel failures.
infographic.paper_title: From Reconstruction to Imputation: Test-Time Optimization for Missing Time-Series Channels

title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
authors: Joey David, Paul Caillon, Alexandre Allauzen
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter's leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter.

infographic.key_insight: The bits needed to preserve fine-tuned behavior depend on the dataset–base-model pair, not simply adapter rank, parameter count, or reconstruction error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate compressed LoRA adapters after reloading them into the target frozen model, since smaller adapters can preserve useful behavior and sometimes reduce corruption-induced damage.
method: Define behavioral rate R* as the smallest serialized adapter size retaining a fixed fraction of held-out fine-tuning gain.
Compare compression rates across training content and frozen base models at fixed optimization budgets.
Analyze data-measured correction spectra and test compression on deliberately corrupted fine-tunes.
infographic.evidence_signal: On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-7B, compression raised a corrupted adapter’s accuracy from 23.7% to 82.9%, versus 77.6% for the frozen base; on harder math, the compressed corrupted adapter retained 97% of base accuracy versus 44% for a clean fine-tune.
infographic.watch_item: Behavioral rate is receiver- and evaluation-dependent, so compression settings and corruption-recovery gains require validation for each target model and task.
infographic.paper_title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information

title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
authors: Quan Minh Nguyen, Hoang M. Ngo, Bhakti Chowkwale, Yasaman Keshtkarjahromi, My T. Thai
abstract: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher weighting.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.

infographic.key_insight: FedFiOT uses Fisher information and optimal transport to align neurons and weight parameter aggregation when merging federated models with limited communication.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets model merging in one-shot and few-round federated learning, where client drift and data heterogeneity can undermine direct averaging.
method: Use Fisher information to estimate parameter importance.
Alternate between optimizing neuron correspondences and global parameters under a shared Fisher-weighted objective.
Prove monotonic decrease of the layer-wise merging objective and derive a stationarity bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over competing baselines across multiple datasets in both one-shot and few-round settings, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Fisher estimation and optimal-transport alignment may add computation and memory overhead; these costs are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning

title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
authors: Michal Korniak, Marco Bagatella, Ralf Römer, Michal Nauman, Yarden As, Pranav Vignesh
abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

infographic.key_insight: Online reinforcement learning can improve generalist robot policies across diverse tasks and, with the right recipe, improve tasks absent from online training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-task adaptation offers a path to improving deployed robot foundation models without restricting optimization to a single task.
method: Develop structured evaluations of multi-task online improvement.
Compare value estimation, policy extraction, and resource allocation choices.
Examine how training-task distributions and value-based RL affect generalization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gains across diverse training tasks and tasks not used during online training, but provides no numerical results or evaluation scale.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization depends on the training-task distribution and RL recipe; improvement on unseen tasks should not be assumed.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement

title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Zhifeng Li, Zhiming Wang, Yongqi Liu, Shanglin Yang, Yang Zhou
abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

infographic.key_insight: Coding agents can autonomously compress LLMs, with the best design per task averaging a 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent-driven compression can reduce model storage while preserving much of baseline performance, but requires independent inference and capability checks.
method: Give agents a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget.
Let agents design compressed weights and inference code using perplexity-guided experiments.
Independently verify final models and evaluate downstream accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six agents and six model–size settings, 29 of 36 submissions passed verification; the best-perplexity designs achieved 77.33% downstream accuracy versus 79.56% for BF16.
infographic.watch_item: Local perplexity gains may not transfer to complete models, and likelihood alone can miss generation and inference failures.
infographic.paper_title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?

title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces
authors: Ben Johnson, Hayden Helm
abstract: Efficient benchmarking estimates a system's full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family- and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system's score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-4}$) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-3}$), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: Structured summaries of cached agent traces enable more accurate benchmark score estimates from very few task executions than correctness-only approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Teams can reduce agent evaluation costs by reusing reference-system traces to estimate full benchmark performance from limited new executions.
method: Use an LLM to extract structured trace summaries, then embed them with a text encoder.
Build low-dimensional system representations that retain task and correctness signals while reducing identity-related signals.
Augment an item-response model with geometry-based score predictions relative to reference systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: With one randomly executed task, mean absolute error fell from 0.13 to 0.08 on SWE-bench Verified and from 0.14 to 0.12 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with Wilcoxon p < 10^-4 and p < 10^-3, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires cached reference traces and an LLM summarization pipeline; generalization beyond the two evaluated benchmarks remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces

title: Message-passing graph persistence
authors: Jorge Luiz Franco, Arthur Queiroz Moura, Moacir Ponti, Amauri Souza
abstract: Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test. Persistent homology (PH) provides topological descriptors that can complement GNN representations, but existing approaches typically compute persistence separately from the representation learning process. In this paper, we introduce Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP), a family of topological descriptors that incorporates message passing into graph filtrations. At each filtration step, node embeddings are updated using the current subgraph and associated with persistence events. These embeddings also determine the representatives of connected components during persistence computation. We prove that MGP is invariant under graph isomorphism and that it is strictly more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends. We evaluate MGP on an expressivity benchmark and on several graph classification and regression datasets. Experiments show that MGP outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of these datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP) integrates message passing into persistent homology to create graph descriptors that are provably more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends.
infographic.engineering_relevance: MGP offers a way to combine learned node representations with topological structure for graph classification and regression.
method: Update node embeddings using the current subgraph at each filtration step.
Associate updated embeddings with persistence events.
Use embeddings to select connected-component representatives while preserving graph-isomorphism invariance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on an expressivity benchmark and several graph classification and regression datasets shows MGP outperforming other PH-based descriptors on most datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Updating embeddings at every filtration step may add computational overhead; the abstract does not quantify runtime or scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Message-passing graph persistence

title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
authors: Siyi Yu
abstract: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

infographic.key_insight: Occupations with higher AI exposure tend to have less dull, dirty, and dangerous work, but accounting for occupational characteristics weakens this association.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Use occupational AI exposure to identify contrasting research settings, not as proof that an AI intervention will relieve undesirable work.
method: Assess working conditions using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations.
Compare LLM exposure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) using equal occupation and employment weights.
Adjust for physical demands, education, training, experience, and wages; separate repetition from restricted discretion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Adjusted confidence intervals for the composite association include zero for LLM exposure but remain below zero for AIOE.
infographic.watch_item: Exposure estimates do not establish workers’ desire for automation or realized relief; both require worker-preference and intervention evidence.
infographic.paper_title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
